title: Dry seasons
hookLine: every practitioner meets seasons when practice feels empty
tomorrow: what did the Buddha tell a town full of doubters?

lines: THE CUSHION AS A WAITING ROOM.
A BONSAI WITH NO NEW LEAVES.
cards: Some mornings the cushion feels like a waiting room: you sit, the timer runs, and nothing happens. Mai has had a whole week of those.

Meanwhile, out on the patio, her grandfather, Ông Thanh, is watering a bonsai that hasn't put out a new leaf since fall. He presses a thumb into the soil, smells the wet dirt, and waters it anyway. Nothing on top.
Something underneath, maybe. The Buddha had a picture for exactly this, and it's a farmer.

teach.b: In a short sutta of the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha describes a farmer with three urgent jobs: plow the field well, sow the seed in time, let the water in and out. That's the farmer's work.

What the farmer can't do, the Buddha says, is command the crop: sprout today, grow ears tomorrow, ripen the day after. The crop comes up when its time comes. Then he turns the picture toward practice.
A practitioner also has urgent work: training in conduct, in the mind, in wisdom. And no one has the power to say: let my mind be free today.

teach.h: THE MIND RIPENS IN ITS TIME.
teach.b: It ripens in its time. It's a humbling picture, and a kind one. That's the Buddhist answer to a dry season.
Not a trick to make the sitting feel full again.
Do the farmer's part: sit, keep the precepts, keep coming back, and stop demanding a harvest on a schedule.
Some teachers call dry stretches an ordinary part of a long practice, not proof that it's failing. A field in winter looks dead.
It's resting. Ông's bonsai is a very small field: a little water, a lot of patience, and roots doing work that nobody sees.

how: Buddhist teachers often encourage practitioners to keep a steady daily sit through stretches that feel empty, keeping the precepts and returning to the cushion without demanding results.

o: stretches when practice feels empty and flat
the hot months when monks travel to teach
the fasting days before a big temple festival

games.q: the farmer's part — tap the pairs.

s: a dry stretch in practice means you're doing it wrong
in the farmer simile the crop comes in its own time; the work is to keep tending.
in the sutta, a farmer who works harder can make the crop ripen faster
he does his three jobs; the ripening isn't his to command.
the Buddha compares freeing the mind to a crop coming up in its season
it ripens when its time comes, not on demand.

games.q: your friend has journaled every night for a month, and lately it feels pointless, just words on a page. what fits the farmer simile?
o: stop for now and wait until the feeling comes back.
keep the small habit going; what's growing may not show yet.
double the time each night until it feels meaningful.
games.why: the farmer plows, sows and waters, and can't order the crop up. keep tending, and stop demanding a harvest on schedule.

practice: If there's a plant near you, press a fingertip into its soil and notice it: cool or warm, damp or dry. If not, press your palms flat on the floor. Then sit the way the farmer waits, the work done and nothing demanded.
When your mind asks whether anything's happening, let the answer be: roots.

wordCard.voice: Dry seasons: stretches when practice feels empty. The farmer keeps plowing and watering, and the crop comes in its own time.

orig.note: Pali: farmer, plowman. The Buddha's picture for a practitioner who tends the field and waits.

carryVoice: Keep sitting: the field is resting, not dead, and the roots are still at work. See you in the morning.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.91 (Accayika Sutta: the farmer's urgent duties; numbered 3.93 in some editions)
